title: Bayesian A/B & Multiple Testing
summary: Answer "how likely is B better, and what do we risk?" with Beta-Binomial posteriors, Monte Carlo P(B > A) and expected loss. Then guard against the two habits that break any test: testing many metrics at once (Bonferroni vs Benjamini–Hochberg) and peeking at a running experiment.
takeaways: Beta is conjugate to the Binomial: the posterior is Beta(α + successes, β + failures). Always include the prior.
P(B > A) and expected loss come from comparing posterior samples. Seed the generator so reports reproduce.
Bonferroni (p ≤ α/m) controls any false positive. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and needs a running minimum to keep adjusted p-values monotone.
Stopping at the first significant look inflates false positives far above α. Fix n in advance or use sequential methods.

steps.label: Prior
steps.detail: Pick Beta(α, β) for each arm's rate. Beta(1, 1) is uniform.

steps.label: Posterior
steps.detail: Add conversions to α and non-conversions to β.

steps.label: Simulate
steps.detail: Draw seeded posterior samples for A and B.

steps.label: Summarize
steps.detail: Compute P(B > A) and the expected loss of each choice.

steps.label: Correct for many tests
steps.detail: Across metrics or segments, adjust with Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg before declaring wins.

terms.definition: A Beta prior on a success probability with Binomial data. The posterior is again a Beta, with the counts added to its parameters.
The probability of a claim (e.g. p_B > p_A) given the data and the prior.
The average amount of the metric you give up by choosing a variant, counting only the cases where it's actually worse.
The probability of at least one false positive among all tests. Bonferroni controls it.
The expected fraction of false positives among the rejected hypotheses. Benjamini–Hochberg controls it.
Repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon test and stopping when it looks significant, which inflates the false positive rate.
